title: The Last Bus
lines: I had my little brother's bus ticket. A second later, I watched his bus pull away without me.
We'd agreed to meet at the market stop. I only had one job, and I'd stopped to check my phone.
I ran toward the shelter, waving my whole arm. The bus went right past the last crossing.
I thought Milo was on it. Then I thought about what he'd do when he realized I wasn't there.
The baker called my name from her doorway. She was holding Milo's blue backpack by one strap.
He'd come in for a cupcake, she said. He left his bag on the chair when the bus came.
I took the bag. Milo always carried a little card with my number, and it was still inside.
I almost ran straight into the road. The baker yelled that the bus made another stop by the park.
The crossing light changed. I went across with the crowd, then ran past the barber and the bookshop.
I could see the park shelter from the corner. It was empty, except for one person looking the other way.
I asked if the bus had gone. He just pointed down the street. It was still turning the corner.
I followed the pavement around the bend. The bus rolled to the curb and put its hazard lights on.
Then Milo stepped down from the door. He was holding a paper wrapper with both hands.
I'd practiced a whole speech on the way over. What came out was, 'I thought I'd lost you.'
He said he told the driver we always sit together. Then he asked if everything in his bag was okay.
I held it up where he could see it. He reached for the strap and finally let himself smile.
He unwrapped his cupcake and gave me half. It had leaned sideways and covered the paper in frosting.
I handed over the ticket. The driver moved his hand off the switch and waited while we climbed in.
We sat on the same side like always. I tucked my phone into the bottom of my own pocket.
The next day Milo carried his ticket. I still walked him to the stop.

title: The Night the Park Went Dark
lines: The court went dark on our last possession. Before I could even see, someone yelled the new kid's name.
Eli lived across from the park. He'd spent three nights watching through the fence before he asked to play.
Earlier that evening, he brought his own ball. He asked which hoop we used, like there was a rule.
When the lights went out, my friend pointed at him. Eli had been nearest to the gate.
I was about to say the same thing. Then he picked up his bag and walked off without arguing.
Someone said we could finish tomorrow. I went to the gate to check if the park was closing.
There was a yellow plug hanging out of the box. I could just see it under the street lamp.
I pushed it back in. The lights came on one at a time, and the ball rolled across the court.
From the gate I could see Eli heading toward the crosswalk. I grabbed the ball and went after him.
I held it out. He took it with one hand and kept looking at the paint on the pavement.
I told him I'd found the plug. He asked if I'd told the others too. I hadn't.
So I went back to the court. My friend was already picking teams like nothing had happened.
I told him about the plug. Then I told him I'd almost blamed Eli too. Nobody picked a team after that.
My friend put his hand down and walked to the gate with me. We called Eli back together.
He looked up this time. He put his bag on the bench and came through the gate with the ball.
We let him take the first shot. He bent his knees, looked once at the rim, and let it go.
It hit the front of the rim and came right back. For a second, nobody said anything.
My friend caught it. Instead of taking his turn, he threw it back to Eli.
Eli asked if he could move a step closer. We all backed up to give him room.
The lights stayed on until closing. When we played again the next day, Eli was the one picking teams.
